title: Catholic: sacred reading
hookLine: read, reflect, pray and rest on one short passage
last: THE SAINTS — A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.

lines: A DAY OF WORDS, NOTHING LEFT.
cards: How do you read now? Honestly. Headlines, captions, the first line of an email, the top of a thread.
Eyes move in a quick zigzag, hunting for the point, and then they're gone. It's efficient. It also means a whole day of words can pass through and leave almost nothing behind.
Now a medieval monk, with one page in front of him, reading it so slowly he's almost chewing it. Today: lectio divina, sacred reading.

teach.b: Lectio divina is Latin: divine reading, or sacred reading. It's old: the Rule of Saint Benedict, written for monks, sets aside hours every day for holy reading.

Much later, a Carthusian monk named Guigo wrote a short letter describing the practice as a ladder with four rungs. The first rung is lectio, reading: slowly, often aloud, a short passage, not a chapter.
The second is meditatio, reflecting: you turn one word or phrase over and over. Guigo uses that very picture: reading puts the food in your mouth, meditation chews it.
The third is oratio, prayer: you respond, speaking to God from what you heard.
The fourth is contemplatio, contemplation: you stop working and simply rest in God's presence, beyond words.
He also puts it this way: seek in reading and you'll find in meditation; knock in prayer and contemplation opens the door. Here's a line to try it on.
Psalm 45 in the Douay-Rheims numbering, 46 in most others: "Be still and see that I am God."

In 2010 Pope Benedict the Sixteenth encouraged the practice for all Catholics, not just monks, and Christians of other churches use it too. The point is not to cover ground. It's to let one short passage cover you.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns set aside time for lectio divina each day, and many Catholic parishes and other Christians use it in groups, often with the Sunday Gospel: reading a passage several times, sharing a word, praying, and resting in silence.

games.q: you've read the verse once. one word catches: still. what does lectio divina suggest next?
o: move on to the next verse.
stay with that word and turn it over.
look it up in a dictionary.
games.why: that's meditatio: chewing one word. then answer, then rest. seek in reading, find in meditation.

practice: Read today's verse four times: be still and see that I am God. First just hear it; then notice the one word that catches, still, or see, or God, and stay with it; then answer it, in prayer if you pray, or in a thought if you don't.
The fourth time, let the words go, and simply rest.

wordCard.voice: Lectio divina. Sacred reading: read, reflect, pray, rest, four rungs of a ladder on one short passage. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: read slowly. A page can be chewed, not just skimmed. Day two hundred sixty-three, done.
